tone_statements.citation: Laman, Karl Edward. 1927. The musical tone of the Teke language. In: Festschrift Meinhof, pp. 118-124. Glückstadt & Hamburg: J.J. Augustin.
tone_statements.quote: In Teke as well as in Kongo we find that one of the most remarkable features of pronunciation is the use of significant musical tones, viz. the pitch of voice with which each syllable is pronounced. [...] Besides these different kinds of tones in Teke there are also others which are used to differentiate fundamental ideas stated by words or phrases (semantic tones). [...] With regard to the tone-series there are in Teke two very distinct tone- series: ahightone-series and a lowtone-series. In each we can dis- tinguish between inherent tone-series and actual tone-series.

sources.citation: Nsuka Nkutsi, François. 1990. Notes sur les parlers teke du Zaïre. Pholia 5: 147-173. Lyon: Laboratoire de Phonétique et Linguistique Africaine, CRLS, Université Lumière-Lyon 2. (fieldwork 1988-89 on four DRC Teke dialects: boma [Boku = South Boma], nkuu, bibaana, teke-sud 'ngi' [Ngi-Puli])
sources.note: p.148: 'la tonalité, l'accent et la morphologie du système nominal présentent des écarts notables par rapport aux dialectes teke du Congo et du Gabon. Nous avons cependant limité notre article à l'examen des sons et des phonèmes' -- accent flagged as notable but explicitly NOT described; sections are 1. sons et phonèmes (C1, C2, *VNC reflexes, vowels, syllable structure incl. final-vowel loss in nkuu/ngi) and 2. liste des correspondances (tone-marked wordlist). No stress/accent placement rule anywhere in pp.147-173.

sources.note: First-hand tone description with phonograph recordings. Teke, like Kongo, uses 'significant musical tones' - semantic tones distinguishing words (ntsa 'antelope' vs ntsa 'fame', bula 'to crush' vs bula 'to strip', i-buli 'I have crushed' vs i-buli 'I have stripped') and tone in declension, conjugation and derivation (inherent/etymological tone vs actual tone in connected speech). sources.citation: Hombert, Jean-Marie. 1986. The development of nasalized vowels in the Teke language group (Bantu). In Koen Bogers, Harry van der Hulst & Maarten Mous (eds.), The phonological representation of suprasegmentals: studies in African languages offered to John M. Stewart on his 60th birthday (Publications in African Languages and Linguistics 4), 359-379. Dordrecht: Foris.
sources.note: Historical study of Teke vowel nasalization; no tone system stated. An accent position in Ibali nouns (after Fontaney & Hombert) is invoked for nasal-consonant loss; the Ibali forms are tone-marked.

tone.quote: The origin of nasalized vowels for the first two groups is clear. In the first case, Froto-Bantu prefixes *ru-, *mi- and *man have become U-, I= and a- (nasalization of v by preceding nasal consonant with subsequent loss of the consonant}. … In Fontaney and Hombert, we argued that the position of an accent accounted for the loss of the nasal consonant in one case but not in the other. The nasalized vowels of the third group are those which are of particular interest here.
tone.summary: Historical study of Teke vowel nasalization; no tone system stated. An accent position in Ibali nouns (after Fontaney & Hombert) is invoked for nasal-consonant loss; the Ibali forms are tone-marked.
tone.says: Historical study of Teke vowel nasalization; no tone system stated. An accent position in Ibali nouns (after Fontaney & Hombert) is invoked for nasal-consonant loss; the Ibali forms are tone-marked.
